/FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Issued at 150 AM MDT Wed Oct 28 2026

A broad, upper-level ridge will sit across the central CONUS Friday 
morning leading to modest southwesterly flow across the region. 
Unlike previous patterns, this ridge will not be as strong and 
temperatures will not warm nearly as much. The next upper-level 
system will be slowly moving into the Pacific Northwest throughout 
much of the day Friday, though its progression will be slow. The 
base of the trough will remain offshore through at least early 
Saturday morning. A very weak shortwave will attempt to push through 
the region on Friday, leading to very weak, synoptic ascent mainly 
across western Nebraska and mainly later in the day as the shortwave 
approaches the region. 700mb slow remains from the southwest and 
fairly weak, with the shortwave barely visible as it progresses 
northeastward and is, ultimately, absorbed into the larger scale 
flow. 700mb temperatures remain in the 4 to 6C range across the 
region throughout the day Friday, so expect temperatures in the 
upper-50s to low-60s everywhere. Surface is currently forecast to be 
out of the south-southeast for all locations east of the Laramie 
Range and out of the southwest for all locations west of the Laramie 
Range. By 18Z Friday the NAEFS Mean Precipitable Water will increase 
to above the 90th percentile for portions of western Nebraska and 
barely into southeast Wyoming before increasing to above the 90th 
percentile nearly everywhere east of the Laramie Range by 00Z 
Saturday. Therefore, moisture will not be a limiting factor as the 
weak forcing moves through, as has been the case for the last 
several systems. The biggest concern will be whether or not the 
ascent from the weak shortwave and systems moving out of the 
southwestern CONUS will be enough to get showers going across 
western Nebraska. If it is, these showers are expected to remain 
rain with snow not anticipated at this time.

Precipitable water values will remain well over the 90th percentile 
for most places throughout the weekend, which may put a small damper 
on Halloween festivities on Saturday evening and night. This 
disturbances off to the southwest will push towards the region on 
Saturday, increasing forcing across the region. The upper-level 
trough over the Pacific Northwest will maintain its slow movement 
inland Saturday, with the trough axis sitting over Idaho and the 
Nevada/Utah border by early Sunday morning. A few lobes of 500mb 
vorticity will eject across the CWA throughout the day Saturday, but 
these look to be weaker than what is expected for Sunday. 700mb flow 
begins to amplify later Saturday into the early morning hours Sunday 
as the 700mb system starts to take shape across western Montana. As 
of now, a strong 700mb jet looks to develop just to the northeast of 
the CWA throughout the evening on Saturday, which would likely 
increase precipitation chances west of the Laramie Range as this 
region remains in the right entrance region of the low-level jet. 
Winds will also likely start picking up Saturday night into early 
Sunday morning for this same region. Luckily, or not if you like 
snow, 700mb temperatures are expected to remain well above the -2 to 
0C range, likely in the 2 to 5C range, which favors any 
precipitation falling as rain and not snow. So what does this mean 
for trick-or-treating and other Halloween activities? Well, as of 
now, precipitation looks to hold off for the most part until early 
Sunday morning, unless you are trick-or-treating in the Snowy Range. 
Temperatures will quickly drop into the 40s for most places by 8PM 
Saturday night, so it looks like there will be a lot of superheroes, 
witches, and vampires with jackets. Luckily, precipitation should 
hold off until festivities end.

Much of the remainder of the long term forecast remains very 
uncertain as model confidence and agreement worsens Sunday through 
Tuesday. The early forecasting shift talked about the possibilities 
in depth, so please read the following for a discussion on the 
Sunday through Tuesday time period...

Forecast confidence decreases considerably as we head into the 
Sunday through Tuesday time period. While there is still potential 
for widespread precipitation, the ensemble spread is enormous as a 
very complex weather pattern sets up over the Western CONUS. First, 
a powerful disturbance will race into the southwest, riding on a 
very strong sub-tropical jet stream. Meanwhile, a northern branch 
trough will dive into the northwest and progress eastward 
simultaneously. The northern upper level low may also close off from 
the polar jet itself, adding to the uncertainty. With so many moving 
parts on the board, it is difficult to have much forecast confidence 
in how this will play out.
